textbookText: mesodermal parenchymatous tissue. 11. Digestive system is incomplete and branched without anus. In tapeworms, digestive system is totally absent. 12. Respiratory, circulatory and skeletal systems are absent. 13. Excretion takes place through special structures called protonephridia or flame cells. 14. Nervous system is primitive consisting of a pair of cerebral ganglia and longitudinal nerve cords connected each other by transverse commisures giving ladder like appearance. 15. Sense organs are simple eye spots or photoreceptor in free living forms but usually absent or reduced in parasitic forms. 16. They are mostly hermaphrodite and very few of them are unisexual. Fertilization is internal which may be self or cross. 17. Parthenogenesis and polyembryony commonly occurs in parasitic forms. 18. Reproduction occurs by sexually and asexually both. Asexual reproduction takes place by regeneration and sexual by fusion of gametes. 19. Development is direct and indirect both. Indirect development is found in endoparasites with many larval forms.

Unique features Dorsoventrally flat body, mostly endoparasites, presence of hooks and suckers in parasitic forms, first triploblastic animals, excretion by flame cells, alimentary canal incomplete or absent, mostly hermaphrodite Classification Phylum platyhelminthes is divided into three classes on the basis of their habitat and digestive tract.

Class 1: Turbellaria i. They are mostly free living, found in freshwater, marine water and moist land. ii. Body is unsegmented, flat, and covered with ciliated cellular layer or syncytial epidermis. Cuticle is absent. iii. Suckers are absent. iv. Alimentary canal is incomplete with eversible pharynx.. v. Touch receptor, chemoreceptor, and photoreceptor are commonly found in free living forms. vi. Mostly hermaphrodite. Reproduction occurs by sexual and asexual method. They have remarkable power of regeneration.

Class 2: Trematoda i. They are commonly called flukes, found as ectoparsites and endoparasites in the body animals. ii. Their body shape is usually leaf like and dorso-ventrally flattened. iii. Outer covering of body wall is cuticle. iv. Digestive tract is incomplete with branched intestine. v. Suckers are usually present to attach with host. vi. They are mostly hermaphrodite. vii. Development is direct in ectoparasites and indirect in endoparasites.
Example: Fasciola (Liver fluke), Schistosoma (blood fluke), Dipolozoan, Gyrodactylus etc.

Class 3: Cestoda (kestos-girdle; eidos-form) i. They are commonly called tapeworms found as endoparasites in the intestine of vertebrates. ii. Body is pseudosegmented, elongated, flat and ribbon like. iii. Body segments are called proglottids which are immature anteriorly, matured at the middle and gravid posteriorly. Each mature proglottid is hermaphrodite. iv. Head or scolex is provided with hooks and suckers. v. Alimentary canal and sense organs are absent. vi. Complicated life cycle involving two vertebrate hosts and embryo is with hooks.

Example: Taenia (tape worm), Echinococcus (dog tapeworm), Hymenolopis (dwarf tape worm) etc. 8.2.5 PHYLUM ASCHELMINTHES Grobben introduced the term Aschelminthes (Gr; askos-cavity; helmins-worm) in the place of older name nemathelminthes. This phylum includes varieties of animals which are either free living or parasitic or epizoic.
1. They are found in aquatic and terrestrial habitat and also as parasites of plants and animals. Some of them are free living forms.
2. They are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, unsegmented, thread like worms having organ system grade of body organization.

3. Body is slender, vermiform and usually cylindrical in outline with indistinct head. 4. They are pseudocoelomate i.e. coelom is derived from blastocoel. 5. Body wall consists of outermost protective cuticle layer, syncytial epidermis without
cilia and a layer of longitudinal muscle. Cuticle layer sheds off periodically.
